_about: planwright worker-settings profile (REQ-F1.8, D-38). A Claude Code settings fragment that a /orchestrate worker (background subagent or headless tmux/cron worker) runs under so the ROUTINE /execute-task toolset is pre-approved and the autonomy loop does not stall on permission prompts. planwright never edits settings.json itself (REQ-I1.2): merge this into the worker's settings (or reference it) the same way hook wiring is a manual step. AUTO-APPROVE HOOK: the hooks.PreToolUse (Bash) entry below wires scripts/worker-command-guard.sh, the deterministic worker command-guard from worker-permission-ergonomics (REQ-C1.1). It reads the Claude Code PreToolUse payload on stdin and extracts the fully-expanded Bash command Claude Code hands it (variables already expanded before the hook runs), then returns permissionDecision: allow ONLY for an enumerated set of known-safe command shapes (read-only coreutils / git / gh, read-only sed and awk scripts, repo scripts and tests, an installed planwright root's scripts/, mise / bats, and control structures whose bodies are themselves verified), deferring everything else to the normal permission flow — so the routine /execute-task toolset stops flooding on the expanded shapes Claude Code cannot statically analyze ($VAR-path script calls, for/while loops). Its properties: no-LLM (pure-shell analysis, no model in the decision path, honoring fleet-autonomy D-18); allow-only (it can ONLY auto-approve — it never emits deny or ask, so it is never worse than today); deny-precedence (a hook allow can never un-block a command the deny block below forbids, because Claude Code evaluates deny before ask before allow regardless of hook output). It references the script through ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} exactly as the plugin's hooks/hooks.json does, so it resolves under a marketplace install, and it is deliberately NOT registered in that plugin-global hooks/hooks.json (REQ-C1.2). WORKER-SCOPED — DO NOT MIS-MERGE: this auto-approve hook stanza belongs ONLY in a dispatched worker's settings (this worker-settings.json), never in a tower or human interactive settings.json, because worker-scoping is enforced only by where the hook is wired, not by any runtime session-type check (REQ-C1.2, R7); merging it into a general ~/.claude/settings.json would silently auto-approve those known-safe shapes in your own interactive and tower sessions — the blast radius D-5 rejects. PLUGIN SCRIPTS NEED NO ALLOW ENTRY: the guard resolves the planwright installation root ITSELF (PLANWRIGHT_ROOT, else CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT, else <claude-dir>/planwright, else its own sibling root — the same chain scripts/resolve-rule-doc.sh and config-get.sh use) and auto-approves `<resolved-root>/scripts/*.sh` after a containment check, so a routine plugin-script call is approved on any machine and across plugin updates with no per-machine setup. OPTIONAL literal-path allow entry: as defense-in-depth for the hook's jq-absent degradation path (where the hook defers everything), an adopter MAY additionally add a persistent Bash allow entry matching the resolved literal absolute path of the plugin scripts their workers invoke (for example `Bash(/abs/path/to/planwright/scripts/*)`); this path is install-location-specific, so it stays adopter-documented rather than shipped (D-7, REQ-D1.1). It is no longer needed for routine plugin-script approval — only for that degradation path. GLOB DISCIPLINE: path-scoped allow entries use the trailing `/*` glob (as that literal-path entry does), never the `:*` command-boundary form — `:*` matches only where a space or end-of-string follows the prefix, so a directory-scoped `:*` rule silently never matches `<dir>/<file>` and never fires (D-6, REQ-B1.3; the `mise run check` guard scripts/check-glob-allow-rules.sh flags it; see docs/overlays.md). SECURITY: this is a permissions allowlist and needs human sign-off before use; the deny block encodes planwright's hard invariants (never merge / force-push / amend / squash / rebase) as guardrails, but review the allow list against your repo's risk posture first. `gh pr ready` is allowed (not denied) so /spec-kickoff can mark the spec PR ready as its terminal step — the narrow exception to bootstrap D-26's all-drafts rule that kickoff-lifecycle D-6 carries (only the spec PR, by /spec-kickoff; task PRs stay drafts; merge stays human, never auto-merge); the permission un-blocks the command, while the only-the-spec-PR scope is enforced by the skill, not the glob. The `gh pr ready --undo` form (both `gh pr ready --undo` and the `gh pr ready <pr> --undo` flag-after-arg spelling) is explicitly denied so a worker can only un-draft a PR, never re-draft one. Deny precedence: Claude Code evaluates deny before allow, so the deny rules below override the broad `git push origin` allow regardless of specificity. The push denies close the known evasions of the force/main guardrails, not just the flag-immediately-after-`git push` form: `git push * --force*` / `git push * -f*` catch force flags placed AFTER the remote (e.g. `git push origin --force`); `git push *+*` catches the `+<refspec>` force form (e.g. `git push origin +HEAD:main`); `git push *:main` / `git push * main` catch the short (`HEAD:main`) and bare (`origin main`) `main` destinations, and `git push *refs/heads/main` / `git push *heads/main` catch the fully-qualified and abbreviated `refs/heads/main` spellings; `--mirror`/`--all` are denied as bulk-ref escape hatches. These are whole-command glob deny rules, so they are best-effort against exotic refspec spellings rather than exhaustive: review them against your repo's risk posture before relying on the fragment. Compound commands are parsed per-subcommand by Claude Code, so a denied push cannot be smuggled via `&&`/`;`/`|`. The documented separator list does NOT cover command substitution (`$(...)`, backticks) and whether the real matcher reaches into one is undocumented and unverified, so treat `git status "$(git push origin main)"` as reaching the githooks/ backstop rather than this glob layer (see the matcher-model doc, boundary MB-7); the earlier flat claim of `subshell` coverage here was not substantiated. WHAT EACH DENY MATCHES IS TESTED, NOT ASSERTED IN PROSE: tests/test-permission-matcher.sh asserts this deny block against a fixture table of real `git push`/`git commit` invocations, evaluated by a documented re-implementation of Claude Code's matcher (tests/lib/permission-matcher.sh). The matcher semantics, the Claude Code version modeled, the sources consulted, and the boundaries and assumptions the model does NOT settle are in docs/permission-matcher-model.md — read that before editing a rule here (guard-coverage Task 1, D-4, REQ-A1.1). The test also fails on a rule no fixture row exercises and on a rule no fixture row depends on, so neither an untested nor a deletable deny can ship. TWO IDIOMS, DELIBERATELY DIFFERENT: flag denies use the bare-`*` form (`git push * --force*`) because a flag name is a closed token, while `main`-destination denies use the word-boundary form (`git push * main *`) so branch names that merely EXTEND `main` (`main-fix`, `maintenance`) stay pushable; the end-wildcarded destination rules are what stop a flag placed after `main` from evading the end-anchored ones. THE HOOK-BYPASS DENIES exist because the githooks/ backstop (guard-coverage D-2) is only an enforcement layer for spellings the glob layer also sees: `git * --no-verify*` and the `git commit -n*` pair (`-n` is `--no-verify` for commit, but `--dry-run` for push, which is why the short-flag denies are commit-scoped), plus categorical denies on every `core.hooksPath` injection spelling git 2.55 accepts — the `git -c` prefix, the standalone `git config` persistent-disable form, and `git --config-env` — each carried in canonical and all-lowercase spellings because git config keys are case-insensitive while these globs are not (arbitrary casings are a recorded accepted residual). `git * --hooks-path*` is forward-compatibility only: git 2.55 has no such flag. The `--amend`/`--squash`/`--fixup` family is denied in both the leading and flag-after-argument positions and in the `=`-suffixed spellings (`--fixup=amend:`, `--squash=<commit>`), which the `:*` rules alone miss because `:*` requires a following space. GLOBAL-OPTION PREFIX FAMILY: `git -* push*` (and the same for commit, merge, rebase, reset, filter-branch, filter-repo) exists because every other rule anchors on `git push`/`git commit` at the start of the command, so ANY git global option in front of the subcommand slipped past all of them — `git -C . push --force origin topic` and `git -c a=b rebase -i HEAD~2` matched nothing (found by the panel review pass, 2026-07-29). git's global-option list is long and growing (-C, -c, --git-dir, --work-tree, --namespace, --exec-path, --no-pager, --bare, ...), so keying on the leading `git -` covers the class in one rule per subcommand instead of enumerating them; the pattern is anchored at position 0, so commit-message content can never trigger it. It also closes the mixed-case hooksPath gap for those subcommands, since it does not key on the config key at all. Accepted cost: a read-only global-option-prefixed command containing a later ` push`/` commit` token (e.g. `git -C /other log -- commit.md`) is denied — fail-safe and recorded, not narrowed.
